subtopic: AUTOMATIC PAROLE REVIEW
AUTOMATIC PAROLE REVIEW
speechtext: Is the government considering the recommendation of the Fauteux report that a system of automatic parole review should be instituted in Canada thereby dispensing with the present system which requires an application for parole and, if not, for what reason?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AUTOMATIC PAROLE REVIEW
speechtext:
The Parole Act, proclaimed in force as of February 15, 1959, provides, at the time prescribed by the regulations, for a review of "the case of every inmate serving a sentence of imprisonment of two years or more, whether or not an application has been made by or on behalf of the inmate". In the

Questions
case of an inmate serving a sentence of imprisonment of less than two years, the obligation to review exists, upon application by or on behalf of the inmate.
The parole regulations became effective on September 1, 1960, and the system of automatic parole review recommended by the Fauteux report came into effect at the same date in the case of penitentiary inmates and of prison inmates serving aggregate sentences of two years or more.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour and ask him what is being done at the moment to bring about the settlement of the strike of the longshoremen of the St. Lawrence ports scheduled for Friday. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend has misinterpreted the statements I made. I feel sure he knows what steps have been taken and what steps are planned to encourage bilingualism in the Department of National Defence and within the three armed services of Canada.
However, in the case of Canadian armed forces taking part in a mission under an international body such as NATO or NORAD,

Inquiries of the Ministry where headquarters are made up of officers from various countries and the forces of several nations are supposed to work together, in order to avoid any misunderstanding from a security point of view, it has been agreed that words of command are to be given in English.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: TAXABILITY OF $500 GRANT FOR WINTER HOUSE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to reply to the question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Ontario respecting the $500 bonus to be paid to the first purchaser of a new house constructed mainly during the winter period.
A person who purchases the house as a personal residence for himself will receive the $500 payment without income tax consequences.
Where the first purchaser rents out the whole or a part of the house or otherwise uses it for revenue purposes, the payment of $500 which he is to receive from the government will reduce the capital cost of the house which is the basis for the capital cost allowance which he may claim for income tax purposes.
Where the first purchaser of the house is subject to tax as a trader in real estate, he will have to take the payment of $500 into his calculation of the profit or loss of the business.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, October 1, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Miss LaMarsh-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Old Age Security Act to increase the pension under the said act from $65 a month to $75 a month, effective October 1, 1963, and to increase the rate of old age security tax from the present rate of 3 per cent with a maximum of $90 to a rate of 4 per cent with a maximum of $120 on the taxable income of individuals, applicable to the 1964 and subsequent taxation years.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Last evening when the committee adjourned I sought to put on the record one paragraph from a publication called, "Policies of the Liberal Party, General Election, 1963." Perhaps I could just read it. The heading is "Establish a new national minimum of $75 a month pension," and it is as follows:
To help people already retired, who have not had the chance to contribute under the new Liberal plan, a minimum supplementary pension of $10 a month will be paid from the start, out of the pension fund established by contributions. This will raise the total old age pension to $75 for a single or widowed person, $140 for a married couple.
Now, when the government considered this matter after the election we came to the conclusion that it was not practical to limit it to $140 for a married couple and that all persons should be treated alike, whether or not they were married, and it should be uniformly set at $75. Up until late August or the beginning of September it was hoped that the government, as was evidenced in the house, could carry out the plan in all other essentials as outlined in this literature. When it became apparent, as it did early in September in the light of developments in two of the provinces, that in order to work out arrangements that would be fair to the public in those provinces and elsewhere in Canada it would take a longer time than had originally been expected, it was then decided to go ahead with the measure that is now being recommended to the house.
The only other point on which I wish to say a single word is this: It was said by several hon. members on the other side, and quite correctly, that the government said this would not be done out of taxes but out of contributions. This is quite correct, as is shown by the passage that I read. Now, sir, when that was put in the literature I think all of us understood quite clearly what that meant. It was not going to be paid out of general revenues, and indeed in one of the other publications we said quite specifically it would not be added to the budgetary
Old Age Security
deficit. Therefore, when it was decided to separate these two measures, it was felt whatever funds would be required to defray this extra $10 should be raised separately and distinctly and be paid into the existing old age security fund. This is what is proposed in this measure. While it is true that, in one sense, that is a tax, it does not go into the consolidated fund but into a separate and distinct fund which can be used only for old age security. It really does, I think, perhaps not fulfil the letter but it does fulfil the spirit of this phrase that the $10 a month will be paid from the start out of the pension fund. It is true it is out of the existing pension fund and not out of the new one. It certainly does not conform with the letter of this paragraph, and I do not think any of us pretend it does.
We have sought to deal with the matter responsibly. While raising the pension, we have sought at the same time to make provision for the raising of the necessary funds to pay this pension so it will not add to the general budgetary deficit of the country.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in speaking on this resolution to amend the Old Age Security Act, I would like to say at the outset that I am in full agreement with amending it in order to bring about an increase in the pension from $65 to $75 per month. However there are one or two things with which I do not agree, and one is that I believe the pension should be made retroactive to April 8.
The other matter, which is of much concern to me and to some old age pensioners in my area, is that while a married couple will benefit greatly from the increase, a single pensioner or a remaining spouse will find it very difficult to live on $75 per month. Actually this is not sufficient. First the cost of living has gone up, and even though single pensioners may own their own homes, their taxes have also gone up. This all creates hardship for the single pensioner.
I am prevented by the rules from presenting an amendment but I would like the minister to give some consideration to this matter. It might be possible to establish a means test so that single pensioners could get more than $75 a month. In the northern area of Saskatchewan which I represent there are many people who will not benefit greatly from this pension increase, and during my stay at

home during the recess I was approached by some of them and was asked to bring this matter to the notice of the minister.
I would like to ask the minister to give consideration to this matter before the bill is introduced, so that it may be possible to devise measures whereby the pensioners to whom I have referred will receive a benefit equal to that received by married couples.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
I have just a brief word to say to the minister concerning something about which perhaps she may not be aware. It has been brought to the attention of myself and a number of other members that there are certain companies in Canada who have former employees on pension, but the pension arrangements are such that if an increase is given in the old age pension these few companies-and I take it that fortunately there are very few-have the unpleasant habit of reducing the pensions they pay to their former employees by the amount of old age pension increase.
I realize the difficulty which the minister would have in doing anything about such a situation, but I hope she would discuss it with the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue. Sometimes there are indirect ways, if not direct ways, of stopping this kind of unpleasant occurrence.
I have a number of letters on my desk dealing with this matter, but I will not take the time to read them. I know other members have received similar letters, and perhaps the minister has also. I hope some consideration could be given to attempting to stop these companies from doing this.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
The matter to which my hon. friend refers was recently brought to my attention by the hon. member for Kootenay East who headed a delegation to me regarding one such company pension program. It will be appreciated that each individual program differs and the legal position depends on the phraseology of each particular program. In this particular instance it appeared that the amount of the pension would be reduced by any contribution which the company might have to make directly or indirectly through taxation; but I would call my hon. friend's attention to the way in which the money for this increase is being raised, that is by way of personal taxation. In my own opinion, although I do not intend to give the house a legal opinion, that company would be unjustified in making a reduction in payment to their pensioners on such a basis.
However, all such contracts may not have the same phraseology, and it may be appreciated that there is no way in which the federal government can interfere in private 28902-5-200
Old Age Security
matters. Certainly such action is frowned upon, and in passing legislation such as this it is the intention of the government, and indeed of the whole house, to pass the benefit on to the old age pensioners, and not in effect to reduce the obligation of a company to pay pensions to those already on pension.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
I am very pleased to hear the minister's comments with respect to this proposal, which has been made by a certain company in the constituencies of Kootenay East and Kootenay West, the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. I am sure she has been well informed of the situation which has arisen there and which has caused serious concern to the pensioners, employees, unions representing them, and many other people in the district who have been rather appalled at the suggestion on the part of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company that, as a result of a certain bylaw in their pension fund, they have the legal right to deduct this $10 if there is an increase in old age security pensions. Therefore I think the minister raised a very good point-it is one that I intended to raise-on the basis of their not being taxed for this increase. In this case, whether we agree with it or not, the proposal in the resolution is a personal income tax increase, and I know the minister has received representations from the representatives of the employees concerned.
I must say I was very pleased to hear her sympathetic approach to the situation. No doubt there is sometimes an advantage in having a lady minister. You can arouse a lady minister's humanitarian instincts when sometimes this cannot be done with the Secretary of State and some others I know. I am sure this statement on the part of the minister will be welcomed by the employees concerned and I trust the government will use its good influences to make certain there is no effect to the proposal of the company as forwarded, to the pensioners a short time ago. The company must see that it is most unfair and has not the support of this government or the members of this house.
Mr. Chairman, I rose just briefly to say how pleased I am that there is this increase of $10 a month. It should be more. It is very necessary. But even the $10 will be very welcome to the thousands of pensioners in this country who have been looking forward to it for some months.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had no intention of taking part in this debate, but since we are on the third day of the debate and I realized that many members still want to express their views, I figured I should do the same myself.

Old Age Security
I see that a matter we all agree on takes several hours of discussion to be adopted even at the resolution stage. I am very sorry about that.
I would particularly like to raise the following points. I would like to talk about the history of the proposal. When the Minister of National Health and Welfare submitted her resolution last spring, it seemed to be linked with the pension plan. At that time, the opposition exerted pressures to have the $10 separated from the pension scheme. During the summer, events forced the government to modify its view and I wish to thank the administration for making the $10 old age pension increase a plan separate from the pension plan. Otherwise, the government would have linked two things entirely different in nature.
Mr. Chairman, yesterday we saw the official opposition ask that the $10 increase be paid retroactive to April 8. I am wondering about their sincerity. Why not make it retroactive to June 22 of last year, when the official opposition was in office, a time when it could have offered that $10 increase to old age pensioners. The government of that time could have relied on our support and would have also been able to rely on the support of the then official opposition. I feel that this $10 increase would have been welcome at the time and we would not have to try and make it retroactive today.
Therefore, I believe that yesterday the gentlemen in opposition did not prove their earnestness in any way.
If we admit that the $10 increase is justified, we must make sure that it is adopted as soon as possible in order that our old people may receive an extra $10 at the end of this month with their regular cheque.
If we admit that the increase is necessary, I feel we should not continue to play politics as was done during the past three days at the expense of the elderly people of this country, who are waiting for us to deal fairly with them.
Mr. Chairman, this increase in the old age pension will be financed through a 1 per cent increase of the workers' income tax. According to the philosophy that we advocate in Social Credit, obviously that old age pension increase would not have been accompanied by an increase of the personal income tax. Where are we going with a system where everything boils down to a tax increase?
The minister said that she had to look for the $118 or $120 million she needs in the taxpayers' pockets. However, I notice that in her general pension scheme, there is a key phrase which, in my opinion, is the substance of the whole program, and that is where she says that the amounts of money
[Mr. Lessard (Lake St. John) .1
which shall be given back to the Canadian citizen upon their retirement, will include the contributions of all the people, less administration costs which have been estimated at about $12 million per year. In short, a dollar will be taken from us and we will get it back years later, less the value of those $12 million in the total amount.
Mr. Chairman, we must ask ourselves what efficiency there is in this procedure. I regret that, in the twentieth century, it is still impossible to finance social security measures in our country without taxing the income of the workers who are growing fewer and fewer. That will inevitably put a heavier burden on each worker.
I am of the opinion that all those increases will discourage the workers from showing initiative and that the government will have to study, as soon as possible, ways of financing the country's administration other than by taxation.
Mr. Chairman, in the private sector there is a growing tendency to prepare budgets according to revenue, that is to say, an estimate of revenue is made and expenditures are reduced so that they may be covered by revenue.
On the other hand, at all levels of government, the opposite is true today, that is to say, governments make an estimate of their expenditures and then look for sources of revenue. Departments prepare estimates of expenditures, sometimes more or less justified, and which do not give the results reasonably expected. And the ministers then ask the house to finance the cost through tax increases.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that this procedure should no longer be followed and that means should be found to finance increased social security benefits without resorting to personal taxation, affecting workers especially.
As a matter of fact, I wonder who the government will tax in the year two thousand, when it is expected that workers will no longer be employed as such, will no longer be paid by industry, or will be replaced by electronic brains? Will taxes be levied on electronic brains then? This is what we should ask ourselves.
Mr. Chairman, I am of the opinion that the resolution should be passed immediately so that the bill may be considered and passed for the benefit of all those who will get the increase at the end of the month.

Mr. Chairman, just before passing this resolution, which could have been passed last night had it not been for the intervention of the Secretary of State-we were ready to go ahead with it and we could have been on second reading of the bill today; it is unfortunate that delay should have occurred -may I rise for a minute or two to make a remark concerning the statement made today by the Secretary of State. I hope it will not pass unnoticed that he has now publicly admitted that which we all knew, that the election literature of the Liberal party this year was inaccurate and deliberately calculated to mislead the public. He has now made this statement in the house, and I hope it will serve as a lesson to his party in the future not to put before the people facts which cannot be verified, and mislead them by inaccuracies such as were displayed in their literature. The fact that he has now admitted this is surely an indication of a change of heart on the part of the Liberal party. But I hope this has not gone unnoticed. Yesterday when we drew attention, through the hon. member for Bow River, to inaccurate statements in Liberal party election literature, it was denied by the minister of national health 28902-5-200i
Old Age Security
and objected to by the Secretary of State, and we produced proof that these inaccuracies occurred in their literature.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to intervene in this debate on the resolution but I feel impelled to do so on account of the statements which have recently been made and the spectacle we had last night. This resolution and the bill it precedes is a matter of great importance to hundreds of thousands of old age pensioners-heart-rending importance. It is also a matter of great economic importance to the whole community. One would have thought it would be possible to discuss the merits of this bill, the material and substantive content of it. But what did we have? We had a debate, if one can dignify the performance yesterday by that word, which resolved itself merely into name calling, into attempting to prove that this cabinet minister said this and that private member said that, and finally degenerated into a most vulgar shouting contest in this house, a display which brought no credit on parliamentary institutions and must have created an extremely bad impression in the galleries of this chamber.
I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that those who have been using this bill as a political football should realize that the old age pensioners of this country are not interested in whether or not this party or that party misled them. They are interested in some relief from the straitened circumstances of their lives. It was perhaps too much to be hoped that hon. members, having raised themselves to the economic level of $18,000 a year in a society that measures all virtue in dollars, would have improved their intellectual contributions in this chamber. After all, intellectual contributions are dependant upon intellectual capacities. But surely it was not too much to hope that having accepted, shall we say with graciousness and a certain alacrity, this generous treatment on the part of the people of Canada, some hon. members might at least have taken some lessons in elementary civilized behaviour. A fool is always difficult to endure. A well-mannered fool is less unendurable than a lout. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that members of this house should bear in mind that the public are watching them, watching them with a very much more critical eye than they did before the recent increase in the indemnities of the members of parliament. I hope that we are not again going to be treated to the disgraceful exhibition to which we were treated yesterday.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

Old Age Security

speechtext:
In the limited
time at my disposal I shall attempt to make a statement outlining the program to be established under this bill. Having regard to the fact that the first resolution to be considered during the private members' hour has to do, I believe, with the problem of older workers, I am wondering whether the committee would not agree to allowing me, if necessary, three or four minutes extra in which to complete this statement so that it may be complete before we continue the discussion at the next sitting of the house.
Vocational Training Assistance Act
On June 10 the minister announced to the house a number of measures which set forth the government's new employment and manpower development program. This program is designed to provide a co-ordinated attack on unemployment, to stimulate manpower development and training, and to increase the employment security of the Canadian work force, particularly during the winter months.
A number of these measures are designed to improve the federal-provincial program of technical and vocational training, particularly in the strategic areas of increasing the training of the unemployed and in stimulating the training of adult and employed workers so that they can adapt to automation and other industrial changes.
Most importantly, the provision of capital facilities for the training of youth and adults under the Technical and Vocational Training Act of 1960 is far from complete in many of the provinces. It is, therefore, important to continue a high level of federal financial assistance to those provinces which still need to develop extensive training facilities.
These amendments to the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act are intended to stimulate greatly the training of the unemployed; to provide for the stimulation of training in industry, particularly where such training is important to the adaptation	of workers to technological
change; and to provide for the extension of capital facilities in the provinces where the needs are greatest.
I should like now to take up the objectives of each of these amendments in more detail so as to provide the committee with a basis for their detailed consideration.
Raising the federal share of training allowance
of unemployed persons from 75 per cent to 90 per cent
The importance of training the unemployed cannot be over-estimated. Basically, a large portion of the unemployed are not suited for the expanding employment opportunities of the Canadian economy because of their relatively low levels of education and skill. Many of them will not be in a position to secure re-employment, until they are provided with new skills and their basic levels of training raised. The necessary stepping up of the rate of training for the unemployed depends on the co-operation and resources of the provinces and of municipalities across Canada. The basic role of the provinces in this program is to provide teachers and training facilities for which they are, of course, reimbursed to the extent of 75 per cent of their expenditures. The proposal that 90 per cent of cost of training allowances be assumed by the federal

Vocational Training Assistance Act government will release needed funds for the provinces to undertake their basic job of providing training programs. The minister would like to see the rate of training of the unemployed reach a level of 70,000 over the next 12 months, from the level of 38,000 which was achieved during the last fiscal year. In addition to providing additional support for training allowances, the government intends to strengthen the national employment service so as to improve selection and placement facilities for those undertaking training programs and to provide every necessary technical support to assist the provinces in improving the techniques for the training of the unemployed. In short, it is the minister's intention to do everything possible to provide effective and balanced training programs for the unemployed in line with their individual needs and those of the economy.
Raising of the federal share of training costs in industry from 50 per cent to 75 per cent
Training in industry is basic to meeting the technological and other needs of the changing industrial scene and in avoiding unemployment which results from technological displacement. Very little has been done under the auspices of the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act to stimulate training in industry, particularly in those areas of training which are not directly related to the short term of occupational needs of employers. Our proposals to amend the act are designed to enable industry to develop those kinds of training which are important to the long run employment security of workers, but which do not yield immediate returns to industry.
The increase to 75 per cent in the rate of the federal reimbursement to the provinces will enable them to provide increased support to the training activities of industry in three strategic areas.
First, the upgrading of the general educational level of the employed labour force through programs of basic training for skill development. This is important if workers' skills are not to become obsolete, resulting in unemployment and income loss.
Second, apprenticeship training programs, which are a basic form of training for the skilled trades, are lagging badly and this increased financing will provide much needed additional support for the development of apprenticeship programs in Canadian industry.
Third, on June 10 the minister announced the introduction of a program designed to assist industry and labour to provide for the development of manpower adjustment programs to meet the needs of changing technology in industry. An important aspect of the

development of manpower adjustment programs is the provision of retraining for workers who will be permanently displaced if they are not retrained. Again, under this amendment we will reimburse the provinces for 75 per cent of industry's costs of conducting retraining programs for potentially displaced workers in the context of a manpower adjustment program.
The third objective is the extension of the 75 per cent contribution in respect of capital costs for training facilities. The Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act provides in section 4 for a contribution by the federal government of 50 per cent of capital expenditures incurred by the provinces in training facilities until the expiry of agreements on March 31, 1967, plus an additional 25 per cent if these capital expenditures were incurred before April 1, 1963. The additional 25 per cent federal contribution in the legislation was intended to act as a special incentive to encourage the provinces to close the gap in vocational training facilities rapidly in the two years from April, 1961, to April, 1963.
This provision of the legislation resulted in an uneven response by the provinces in meeting their needs for training facilities. The plans of some of the provinces were much more advanced than others at the beginning of the period. Today the provinces stand in an unequal position with respect to the degree to which they have succeeded in meeting their needs for vocational training facilities.
The approved federal contributions to capital expenditures up to March 31, 1963, on a per capita basis in the age group 15 to 19 years, indicate that there is substantial variation among the provinces. This figure ranges from $51 per capita in Quebec to $480 in Newfoundland. For Canada as a whole the per capita average is $225.
These variations in the per capita contribution per person in the student age group represent substantial differences in the extent to which the provinces have been able to meet the needs for increased training facilities. This is not to say that the need on a per student basis is equal in each of the provinces but rather that there exists at present considerable inequality in the outstanding needs of the provinces for additional training facilities. The government is proposing, to enable these provinces which have not as yet undertaken building programs sufficient to meet their needs, that the 25 per cent additional contribution be continued on the following basis, which will be provided for in the amendment to the legislation.
The highest per capita federal contribution approved up to March 31, 1963, is $480, which sets the top standard for the federal

contribution on a 75 per cent basis. This happens to be the case for the province of Newfoundland. It is proposed that other provinces be allowed to meet this per capita standard of $480 so that the additional federal contribution of 25 per cent will be continued in each province until the per capita of federal payments in the province has reached this standard of $480, or until expiry of the present agreement on March 31, 1967, whichever is sooner. Once the $480 per capita standard has been reached in a province, they will, of course, be eligible for a continuing 50 per cent contribution to capital until the end of the agreement.

subtopic: ENCOURAGEMENT OP EMPLOYMENT OF OLDER PERSONS
ENCOURAGEMENT OP EMPLOYMENT OF OLDER PERSONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the establish-

Labour Conditions
raent of appropriate measures to encourage the employment of persons over the age of 40 in business and industry.
He said: I believe, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps one of the greatest problems faced by most members of this house, and one of the most difficult problems, is requests for aid from constituents who are over the age of 40 and who find difficulty in obtaining employment. This problem, of course, has existed for a good many years. I believe it has been aggravated and accelerated very greatly since the conclusion of world war II. There are several reasons for this. The first is the increased rate of automation in industry, where hand labour is more and more becoming less and less important. Many persons who are in their forties or fifties, and who have learned to do one thing during their lives, find they have been displaced. They feel they are unable to learn a new trade at this age. They feel at a loss, and do not know what to do.
Another reason that this matter is becoming more aggravated since world war II is the terms of some pension schemes that we find in industry. This has particular reference, of course, to the cost of these schemes. The third reason is the extension of the human life span in the last 25 years or so. Formerly people used to live perhaps only to 55, 60 or 65. The life span has been greatly extended, of course, and this should affect our thinking about retirement age. Certainly during the depression of the thirties, it was felt these people should retire to make work available for younger people. This thinking is pretty well outdated now. People live very much longer. A great many people at the age of 65, so I am told, do not feel a bit like retiring. They are quite capable of carrying on useful work and perhaps, in some cases, better able to do their work as a result of the experience they have gained.
These are three reasons that I believe have aggravated ths problem since world war II. If I may repeat them, they are, one, automation; two, the terms of many company pension schemes; three, the extension of the human life span which has not changed the thinking of people but should have changed the thinking of people in respect of retirement age. This subject has been brought before the house by myself and other hon. members on various occasions within the last ten years. Some of these members are here today and some are no longer with us. I have dealt with this subject at great length on previous occasions, so I do not believe I should repeat what I have said in the past and so waste the time of the house. Today I wish to bring forward some new ideas and suggestions for dealing with this subject. For those

who are interested, I may say that I dealt with this subject previously and my speech is recorded in volume 1 of Hansard lor 1959, page 526. I mentioned one thing at that time to which I should like to refer now. If I may say so, Mr. Speaker, I think I put the matter rather succinctly at the time and as it is rather important background material, I shall, therefore, take the liberty of quoting myself for a minute or two.
The fact that the Canadian population is growing older, coupled with trends which result in the reduction or withdrawal from employment of important proportions of our older workers, constitutes a very grave national problem that requires the closest scrutiny, not only from all levels of government but from labour, industry and private individuals as well.
If I may elaborate on that briefly, Mr. Speaker, I would say this is not the prime responsibility of the federal government by any means. It is the responsibility of provincial governments, labour groups, employer groups, and indeed the public at large.
It is very interesting to note that in 1881 the number of Canadians over 40 comprised about 20 per cent of the population. By 1951 they had increased to about 33 per cent. When we consider this trend in relation to the fact that one of the chief difficulties facing the national employment service in matching unplaced applicants with unfilled jobs is the tendency on the part of employers to reject applicants over 40 years of age, one major aspect of this increasingly grave problem is illustrated.
Again, if I may refer briefly to the population figures in 1881, we see that there were 15 adults under 65 years of age to every 1 over 65, whereas today there are only 7 adults under 65 to every 1 over 65. By 1970 it is estimated the proportion will be over 5 to 1. When we consider the effect of the trend toward more pension plans with the compulsory retirement age now normally set at 65, another major aspect of this problem is seen. We are confronted with the problem of whether or not it is economically possible to maintain a high standard of living here in Canada in the face of trends which show an increasing number of older people retired or withdrawn from the productive section of our economy. At the same time the effect of this trend is to reduce their ability to consume goods, and to place the burden of production and taxation upon a decreasing percentage of the population. This trend is not likely to change. I am not including in these remarks those older workers who through ill health or personal desire wish to withdraw from the labour force. I am dealing solely with those older workers who wish to work and who either cannot obtain employment or are forced to retire.

Apart from the economic factors involved in this matter, severe social problems are also created. When older persons cannot obtain employment or are forced to retire, many feel that society has no further use for them and they become depressed and dejected. Older persons in this group who have not developed hobbies and other interests during their lives are often left completely alone; their families grow up and their friends either move away or pass away. If such people could work their time would be occupied and they would feel they were doing something useful. Without the work which they desire, there is often very little left but the feeling that they are a burden on society.
There are reasons given for the present resistance by business to hiring older workers, and I would like to refer the house to two surveys made in this regard. One report has been prepared by the information branch of our Department of Labour. This was in 1952, and while there have been some additions to it since then, it is a very complete work and I would commend it to the attention of hon. members.
Another report on this matter was prepared by the Ontario department of public welfare, and it refers to a survey made in the United States, known as the Seven Cities Survey. It was made in seven major industrial cities contiguous to the Canadian border where conditions are very similar to those in Canada.
Both reports set out a number of reasons for this resistance by business to hiring older workers. In my previous remarks I have referred to these reasons at some length. I do not intend to repeat them here, except very briefly to enumerate a few of them.
One of the reasons given by business is that it cannot maintain normal production standards with older workers. In one survey 22.4 per cent of the businesses queried gave this as their reason.
Another reason was that older workers could not meet company physical requirements. Some 20 per cent of the businesses questioned gave that reason. A third reason was that older people are inflexible and set in their ways. Thirteen per cent gave that as their reason, but only 10 per cent gave pension and insurance costs as the reason for not hiring older people. The public normally believe that older workers are not hired because of pension plan costs, but apparently only 10 per cent of the businesses questioned gave that reason, and this is quite interesting.
I might say that these figures which I quote are taken from the Seven Cities Survey. A number of other reasons of less importance are also given, but I will not deal with them.
The survey made by our own Department of Labour says that employers are prejudiced 28902-5-201
Labour Conditions
against hiring older workers because these workers will not adapt to learning new techniques, second because of absenteeism through ill health, and third because older persons slow down and lessen activity.
It also says that company training programs call for the hiring of young people and for the development of their talents over the years, and that it would be unprofitable to invest in the training of older employees. It also says pension plans prevent companies from hiring workers of advanced age, and experience showed that in certain instances younger employees were preferred, such as waiters and waitresses, and sales people. Finally it adds as another reason, pension plans which compel workers to retire at an arbitrary age regardless of their fitness to carry on. These are the principal reasons given as a result of the surveys made in this country and the United States into the objection of companies to employing persons over the age of 40 years.
On careful examination it has been found that not one of these reasons is completely valid. Although many of them have varying degrees of validity others are purely fictional and have no validity at all. For instance, one of the reasons given is that older persons slow down and lessen productivity, but a very careful study which was made of this in Canada and the United States has shown no difference at all between people of 17 and 71 years in the amount of work they can do under "moderate" working conditions. "Moderate working conditions" means conditions prevailing in most modern industrial plants.
Another reason given was that people often prefer to have young people wait on them and work for them, but this is certainly not always the case. Very often when one goes into a store he might prefer to have an older person, experienced in handling a product, wait on him.
Something which has given rise to this problem, which I might mention here, is that since world war II, and particularly through the advertising business on this continent, there has been promoted the idea that all workers are young, beautiful girls and healthy, robust young men. This creates an image in the mind of employers that this is what the public expects and wants to see. In many service industries this is true, and it is most unfortunate that such an image has been created.
This brings us to the question of what has been done so far by the federal government, and over the years a great deal has been done by the government to help alleviate the problem.

Labour Conditions
First I would mention the national employment counselling service tor older workers. People in the older age categories with difficulty in obtaining work can obtain advice and counsel from officials of the national employment offices. This is a very good thing and very helpful.
Second, there is the public education undertaken by the federal Department of Labour. This has been done by trying to persuade the public that it is a good thing to employ older workers, and it has done much to remove the prejudice against employing such people. The department, through its public relations and information branches, has done a good job in this respect.
Third, there are the technical and vocational training courses which were set up under the former minister of labour (Mr. Starr), by which persons out of work are provided with vocational and technical training in order to help them obtain employment.
In this regard the federal-provincial plan for building technical and training schools all across the country has been of great effect, not only in helping to educate young people coming into the labour market but in providing courses for those who are unemployed and requiring additional training.
Those are three things which have been done, and now there is the portable pension plan which has been a matter of some controversy in the house. For that reason I do not wish to deal with it at this time. Certain of the provinces also have similar plans, but undoubtedly when some plan is worked out it will also help matters very greatly in respect to the problem of older people finding employment.
The last thing I want to mention in this regard is something which the present Minister of Labour has introduced and which is also a very commendable scheme. It has not come into effect yet, but when it does on November 1 outright payments will be made to industrial plants which employ persons over the age of 45. As I understand it, during the three months from November 1 to January 31 next, companies taking on workers over age 45 will be given an outright grant of 50 per cent of the wages paid, or $75 a month, whichever happens to be the lesser. These payments will continue for 12 months. The onus will be on companies and workers to prove certain information.
First of all, a company will have to prove that it has not fired some younger person and hired an older one in order to get the subsidy. Further a person being employed has to have been unemployed for six months, must be receiving no benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act, and must have

no other pension. This is certainly a step in the right direction and the minister is to be commended on introducing the scheme.
Despite all these various things that have been done, and that are being done by the federal government, the problem is still very acute indeed. I think, Mr. Speaker, as I pointed out earlier in my remarks, it will probably increase rather than decrease over the next few years because of the trend toward an increased percentage of aged people in the population. Something more has to be done than has been done to date, and something more than is being done at the moment must be done to meet this problem. Certainly a great deal is being done to benefit the younger workers who are coming into the labour force, with all the new education schemes, technical training, and so on. This is very commendable because it will help solve the problem in the future, but to date very little has been spent on older workers.
Like most hon. members of this house I do not approve of subsidies in principle, but I think subsidies can perform a very useful service to meet a temporary emergency. While one might not like to describe assistance to older workers in this way, it is in fact a type of subsidy. One might as well meet these arguments head on and say that in the case of emergency-and I think this is an emergency-some form of subsidy or assistance should be given to older workers who through no fault of their own cannot get employment. I feel it is a valid criticism of the program of the present administration that temporary or seasonal measures are not a complete answer to assisting older workers. They are all very helpful as far as they go, but they are not a complete answer. We are faced with this problem 12 months a year, not three months a year. While I agree it is sometimes wise to try something for a short period of time to see how it works, nevertheless I think there should be long range planning and thinking in this regard. Those in government should be making some provision to assist older workers on a longer range basis than just the three months included in the plan of the present Minister of Labour.
I know that other hon. members will wish to make some remarks on this subject, Mr. Speaker, and I will try to conclude my remarks very briefly. There are a number of suggestions I should like to make for the consideration of the present government as additional ways of meeting this problem. The first is a more intensive advertising campaign by the Department of Labour. I know that to date there has been some public relations and information program in this regard, but it has not been nearly enough. It should be much,

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank hon. members of the house for their courtesy in this regard. I will try to conclude my remarks in about two minutes. First of all, as I mentioned, there should be an advertising campaign by the Department of Labour. I think this advertising campaign should emphasize the following items. First, there are the positive benefits of hiring older workers, those likely to encounter less absenteeism and who very often are more conscientious and more stable. Second, the false prejudice and myth about hiring older people should be exploded by a good, strong advertising campaign. Third, persons who are over the age of 40 at the present time should be encouraged to take training in vocational courses which are available to them. A great many older people feel they do not want to go back to school, but with a good advertising campaign I think they could be encouraged to do this.
The fourth thing which I think should be advertised in such an advertising campaign is that it should emphasize to the public that it is in the public interest to hire older workers, and I think it is a public duty to do so. As a matter of fact there could be some sort of slogan, such as, "If you are not over 40 yet, you soon will be and this might affect you too". This is just the kind of slogan that might be used to bring to mind the fact that everybody can be affected.
The second thing that I think should be done, apart from advertising, would be the giving of tax incentives to encourage companies to alter their present pension plans and retirement schemes and replace them with new ones so that compulsory retirement will not be at the age of 65. I realize this would take some working out but this is the principle I have in mind. As I say, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take up the time of the house by going into this question in detail. I think companies could be encouraged by tax incentives to change a number of their present pension plans which force retirement at the age of 65.

I will not take the time of the house to go over this matter again. I would just mention the question of tax credits or deductions from taxable income of corporations. This could be done on a 12 months basis and would encourage the retaining, rehiring and employing of (a) persons over the age of 65 and (b) a similar scheme for persons over the age of 40, not in that case for rehiring or retaining but for anyone just hiring persons over the age of 40. I know this is giving a preference to people in that age group; you are now considering older workers, but in this case, because of the present problem I think such measures would be necessary for the time being.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I shall conclude my remarks at this stage in order that other hon. members may have an opportunity to speak on this subject. With regard to the question of tax credits, this matter was dealt with in some detail in my previous remarks and those who are interested can refer to Hansard for the details.

subtopic: ENCOURAGEMENT OP EMPLOYMENT OF OLDER PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) for the remarks he made with regard to the problems of the older worker. I must agree with him to some extent, probably to a great extent, with regard to the suggestion that this is one of those problems which has really to be considered by all hon. members of this house as one that is not partisan and is completely devoid of politics. I think the hon. member showed this in his remarks and I commend him for it.
The continued growth and prosperity of any country depends to a large extent on whether industry makes the best use of available manpower. It is vital that an industrial nation like Canada fully utilize its human resources. One of the greatest barriers, as the hon. member for Oxford has stated, facing older people is that it is the policy of many employers to refuse to hire persons in the older age group regardless of whether or not they are capable of doing an efficient job. In some cases even men and women as young as 35 in my own riding have been rejected as being too old.
The belief held by many employers that a worker who has passed the age of 40 is no longer able to maintain production standards is a fallacy. It is an indictment, I believe, against our social system that workers in the over 40 age group should be deprived of gainful employment, regardless of ability and job qualifications, simply by reason of age. It

Labour Conditions
has been said that the twentieth century belongs to youth. Increasing mechanization and the use of high speed machinery has quickened the tempo of industrial life and given added importance to youthful qualities. In the minds of many people, including some older persons themselves, the belief has arisen that once the bloom of youth has faded, rapid mental and physical deterioration begins. One need only to look around this chamber, Mr. Speaker, to see this is not so. This belief has spread to the labour market and has created discrimination in employment against older persons. Thus we have what has been called "the problem of the older worker", the majority of this group being in the 40 and over age bracket.
Canada's population has aged during the first part of this century. This has been shown by studies. This trend is likely to continue in the years ahead. These changes have affected Canada's labour force in that more than one third of Canadian workers are 40 years of age and over, and this age group will continue to increase in number. Further, young people are entering the labour market in increasing numbers due to the high birth rate of the last 15 or 20 years.
Maintaining an age balance in a company's work force is an important part of manpower planning. Many Canadian companies have been able to reduce the effects of automation and technological changes on their employees because of an age balance in their work forces, and lay-offs have been limited because planned retirements took care of the reduction in workers.
Efficient operation can result from the blending of the strength and ability of youth and the experience and judgment of mature workers. Hiring on the basis of ability, not age, can bring about a proper balance. A worker's qualifications and personal suitability are two important and main factors upon which an assessment of ability can be made.
All workers, regardless of age, have special qualities which can be useful to employers; these attributes are found in all age groups and depend largely on the individual. Young people, Mr. Speaker, generally offer speed, physical strength, agility, ambition and vigour. Older workers generally offer mature judgment, knowledge gained by experience, stability, low turnover, less absenteeism, as mentioned by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), and lower accident rates-qualities, Mr. Speaker, which can reduce costs and are essential to the success of any enterprise.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us look at and consider some of the common obstacles to the hiring of persons past the age of 40 years and ask ourselves if these statements are correct. First, frequency of illness increases
[Mr. Macaluso.l
as we grow older; therefore, there is more absenteeism among older workers than among younger workers. Second, physical deterioration is synonymous with age; therefore, older persons are accident prone. Third, age has a direct bearing on insurance rates; therefore, the cost of pension plans mounts excessively with each new participant over 40 years of age. Fourth, as people grow older their ability to learn decreases; therefore, it is harder to train older people in new industrial methods and techniques. Fifth, a person over 40 is not as productive as he was at 20. And last, the cost of pension plans increases in proportion to the number of older workers hired, and pension plans are so set up that companies cannot accept anyone past a certain age; also many companies state that they would be happy to hire older workers except that, since they cannot enter the plan or can contribute for only a few years, it would mean turning them out at 65 with either no pension or one that is inadequate. These statements, Mr. Speaker, are in effect commonly known as "the myth of the older worker".
When is a worker an "older worker"? Although there are different points of view which may provide different answers to this question the following definition has been suggested: "The worker may be regarded as an older worker when his employability begins to become more limited because of his age". From studies which have been made it would seem that about 31 per cent of the unemployed persons in Canada at any given time are over 40 years of age and many experience prolonged periods of unemployment. Conclusive evidence that we generally subscribe to this myth that older workers are second rate employees can be found in the want-ad columns of any metropolitan daily newspaper. A study shows that over 51 per cent of classified advertisements stated definite age restrictions.
Many companies, Mr. Speaker, suffer heavy costs of labour turnover in certain job areas. Much of this recurring loss can be halted by the hiring and retention of mature workers who are more inclined to stay with the job than their younger counterparts. Industrial studies have shown in a comparison of workers over 50 with those under that age that: first, in most occupations productivity often reaches a peak in the 50's; second, older workers are less frequently absent through ill-health and fewer accidents; third, that the learning processes do not appreciably decrease; and last, that there is nothing inherent in the nature of a pension plan which makes it impossible to hire an older worker.

In many companies, it is a company's employment policy, not the pension plan itself which stands in the way of hiring older workers.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, the myth of the older worker has become very important to all Canadians. At one end of the scale, age prejudice cuts off work to increasing numbers of Canadians, while at the other end, education keeps more and more young people in school for longer periods of time. In between these two, a diminishing proportion of wage earners are maintaining the balance and are paying the bills for the many. A more even distribution of costs can be achieved through the employment and retention of more older workers.
Let us consider cutting the cost of labour turnover in industry. Canadian employers can cut their costs of labour turnovers by the hiring of the older worker, for there is less turnover among older workers, once they are employed, than among younger employees. Studies show that the worker 40 years of age and over quits his job less than one half as often as a younger worker. Further, the older worker is fired from his job less often than a younger worker. If an older worker obtains a regular job, he is more likely than a younger person to stay with the firm up to the age of normal retirement; thus older workers are better employment risks than younger persons.
There are many areas, Mr. Speaker, where the older person can readily fit into industry. There are highly skilled supervisory positions in which experience is a prime requirement. Further, there are clerical positions, repetitive jobs and jobs which offer little in the way of a career for younger people, and many other casual work positions which are more suitable to the temperament and abilities of older workers.
Further, Mr. Speaker, the older worker is just as capable of learning new processes and skills as a younger person, yet industry reserves training positions almost exclusively for youth and in doing so increases labour turnover. Industry and business can ill afford to pay the price of age prejudice.
With respect to the learning process, I submit that no one age group has a monopoly in the world of learning. Scientific studies, Mr. Speaker, have shown that generally man is intellectually more able at 50 than he was at 20; and I repeat we need only look around this chamber, Mr. Speaker. Contrary to general belief, the ability to learn does not decrease with age. It is quite possible to learn new skills, even in the twilight of life. Speaking on the mental ability of elderly people, Dr. E. J. Steiglitz, U.S. medical expert on the aged, said:

The hair may stop growing and the pate become a polished dome fringed with silver, but the mind below this shining cupola can continue to grow in understanding, wisdom and appreciation of life.
A Canadian study in the retail trade lends weight to the fact that older persons can readjust, and in the light of this evidence it is time that industry and business accept the fact that it is possible to learn at any age and that learning ability is not the exclusive property of any age group.
Contrary to popular belief, the older worker is less prone to accidents and less likely to be absent than the younger worker. The accident and absenteeism records of older workers are reasons in themselves why the older worker should be welcomed by employers. The absenteeism rates of workers show marked improvements after age 45, and at the same time, are less prone to accidents.
Any industry concerned with the reduction of direct and indirect costs of absenteeism is hardly doing itself a service when it refuses to hire older workers. Studies have shown that the people under 20 have the highest absenteeism rate and every age group above 50 workers lose fewer days on the job than in any age group below 50. I ask, why? I submit it is because of his more highly developed sense of responsibility towards his house, his family and his job. Studies of accident rates give a similar picture-the older worker is less accident prone than the younger worker. Here again is an area where industry can save money. A study by the workmen's compensation board of Ontario shows a marked drop in the number of non-disabling accidents after the age of 40 as compared with the age group 20 to 24.
All this, Mr. Speaker, shows that there is no truth in the claim that older workers are poor employment risks because of absenteeism and accident rates. Hiring on the basis of ability, forgetting about age, will give industry the chance to tap this reservoir of high quality labour with its excellent records of punctuality and steadiness.
Now let us discuss the plan from the argument that these people over 40 cannot fit into a company's pension plan. Few of the problems associated with pension plans as they affect the employment of older workers are insurmountable. I quote, Mr. Speaker, from a study of Canadian pension plans:
The restrictive clauses incorporated in some plans would appear to stem more from employment policy than from pension policy.
The increase in cost from hiring of a limited number of older workers is likely to be insignificant in relation to a firm's total pension costs. Any extra cost is likely to be more than offset by the productivity and general stability of older workers, with their

Labour Conditions
better records in the costly matter of absenteeism, accidents and labour turnover.
Pension plans are classified into two main groups:
(a)	Unit benefit plan. Under this plan the employer must contribute more for the older worker; the employee contributes a fixed percentage of his earnings, regardless of his age. The employer pays the balance of the cost of providing the worker's pension and this involves a higher payment for those in the upper wage brackets. This would apply equally to contributory plans and non-contributory plans.
(b)	Money purchase plan. Under this plan both the employee and the employer contribute an agreed percentage of the employee's earnings and the cost to the employer is the same whether he hires older or younger workers.
A method used to reduce the higher cost is to make special provisions which allow the older worker to increase his percentage contribution to the unit benefit pension plan while maintaining the employer's contribution at the usual level. This could be made a condition of employment and would be a small price for the employee to pay in order to obtain steady employment. At least, he should be given the chance to make that choice.
The federal government pension study, completed in 1957, recommended the removal of age restrictions from pension plans and the removal of the waiting period before entry into a pension plan or a system whereby the employee could make retroactive payments into the pension fund to cover the waiting period.
Many companies use the fear of bad public relations arising from retiring an employee on an inadequate pension as one of their main arguments against hiring older workers. However, they seem to overlook the fact that it is probably worse public relations to become known as an employer who denies men jobs because they are over 50 and cannot join the company's pension plan.
The method which can be used to overcome this fear of bad public relations is to tell the older worker when he is hired that the few years of service he will have by the age of 65 will give him only X dollars of pension and that he must make other arrangements for retirement.
However, the most effective way of overcoming the problem related to pension plans and the employment of older workers is to develop a system of portable pensions. There is no simple solution to the pension problem as it relates to older workers; the present inflexibility of pension plans is detrimental
[Mr. Macaluso.l
to the effective use of our manpower resources. In this respect, the policy of the present government is in the right direction -to bring about a portable pension scheme which is, I believe, the objective of all members of this house.
Refusing people over 40 an interview or a job because of their age aggravates a social and economic problem as the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) has said. Is it economically possible to have an improving standard of living if increasing numbers of older persons are rejected or forced prematurely to withdraw from the productive section of society?
Effects on the individual are felt by the whole community. The male older worker is likely to be the head of a family; his children will probably be of secondary school or college age. If he is not continuously employed, his children may have to stop their education prematurely and he and his wife and family may have to cease participation in community affairs. If he is not steadily employed during his middle years, he is more likely to become a welfare case, with a consequent drain on the public purse, by the time he is 65. The decrease of purchasing power is a factor which can add to the spreading of unemployment generally. Therefore, it is in the social and economic interest of every community, quite apart from the humanitarian aspects, to keep its mature workers as steadily employed as possible.
There is also to be considered the effect of unemployment on the individual of advancing years. With each rejection in his search for employment, his morale is lowered, he begins to think of himself as a forgotten man, unwanted by a society to which he may have devoted himself for many years. He meets rebuff after rebuff from employers and he finally believes that they must be right-that he is too old. He loses confidence in his own ability and the result is a loss of desire and initiative.
Much has been said and written about the employment problem of the older worker. There are really two distinct problems, each requiring a different kind of treatment. First, there are those men and women of advanced years who are no longer physically capable of carrying on in their customary occupations. Most of these are 60 years of age or more, but many years of productive capacity remain for them if the proper job can be found. The treatment here is the rehabilitation of the individual worker. Learning by older people need not be limited to those of professional pursuits or scholarly bent. One can learn to

do creative things of many kinds. We should combat like the plague the notion that older people are too old to learn.
In a second category are those workers who are described as "the too old at 40 group"- a group of people who at the peak of their productive capacity experience difficulty in finding employment solely because of chronological age and the policy of many employers to refuse to hire persons in these upper age groups regardless of whether or not they are capable of doing an efficient job. The treatment here lies in changing the attitude of employers and in rehabilitating the employer rather than the worker.
Chronological age is not a sound foundation upon which to build hiring policies, because it gives no indication of a person's ability, skills or knowledge. The economy of this country cannot remain healthy if human resources are not properly utilized, and this means that no one age group can be given special privileges to the detriment of another, whether it is youth or older workers.
Canadian employers would do well to examine more carefully the abilities of older workers. By maintaining arbitrary age limits and hiring, which automatically bar the older worker from an interview, employers are narrowing the chances of obtaining the right person for the job. The qualities sought in a good employee are as prevalent among the over-40 workers as they are among workers in any other age group.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the sponsor of the motion who enables us again today to study the problem of unemployment, especially in the case of workers over 40 years of age.
The hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) mentioned elderly persons. In my opinion, one cannot say that a person over 40 is old. Otherwise, considering the house, we certainly pass for old people, since members are 40 and yet, their experience enables them to make an interesting contribution.
We wish to help people 40 years of age and over to readily find a position. Now, the government has recently, through the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen), submitted an interesting measure, providing as it did for a special allowance to those who hire workers who are 45 or over and who have been employed for a certain period during the winter months. This step should encourage contractors and industrialists to prefer hiring a man of 45 or more when he needs work.
Labour Conditions
Obviously, a man over 40 may be handicapped because of the fact his pension will be more expensive to his employer, but we must not attach too much importance to that fact considering the huge advantage of his experience. Last year I personally stressed that point of the experience acquired by the worker of 45 or over, because having had some experience in industry, I can re-affirm before this house without any fear of making a mistake that a worker aged 45 or more constitutes a real asset for industry because in addition to being an experienced worker he is responsible and is really devoted to the interests of the firm to which he contributes through his efforts. In my opinion that advantage alone should lead employers to think twice when selecting employees and it should prevent them from considering that a man of over 40 constitutes a liability because his pension would be more expensive, for they will derive in so doing, advantages which will more than make up for that.
Now, all those steps to give assistance to people 40 years old and over by finding jobs for them are only a temporary remedy, a poultice, because in my opinion there is only one true solution, and that is a progressive economy offering employment to all workers anxious to work. It is not by increasing such measures of assistance that we will be able to create a progressive economy.
I am pleased to call attention to the assertion by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso), who says that senior people do not work because there is less purchasing power and, as a result, more unemployment. So, he admits that a lack of purchasing power on the part of the people is a direct cause of unemployment in our country. I thank him for this assertion which confirms what we, in this corner of the house, have repeated for years.
It is useless to be oversubtle. Therefore, let us provide the purchasing power in Canada and instead of increasing Canadian production, let us increase the purchasing power for that production.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that here is the core of the problem, and that it is useless to look for a mere poultice. For a good many years we have had governments which offered a great many poultices. I think that the most efficient of those poultices in the past five years has been the winter works program. Yet, it was a mere poultice, and after applying it for five years, conditions have become quite impossible and intolerable. Consequently, Mr. Speaker, poultices are hardly a desirable thing and, to my mind, all suggested legislation, once applied, proved a mere temporary remedy. What we want in

Labour Conditions
this house are permanent formulas, enabling us to solve the unemployment problem.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that the day when there will be a job for every worker in Canada the problem of the older people of 40, 45, 60, 65 and even 70, will disappear. Indeed, I remember that, during the war, that problem did not come up, because all those people, even if they had only one arm [DOT]-and some of them even lacked both arms -had some job or other which helped Canadian productivity.
So, Mr. Speaker, let us give a new upsurge to our Canadian society by producing for Canadians what Canadians consume, and we shall, by such action, solve every problem now facing this country. Let us not lose any more precious time in looking elsewhere for a solution.
